Tl;dr: I’ll try here to show how CFAR’s “art of rationality” has evolved over time, and what has driven that evolution.

In the course of this, I’ll introduce the distinction between what I’ll call “reality-revealing puzzles” and “reality-masking puzzles”—a distinction that I think is almost necessary for anyone attempting to develop a psychological art in ways that will help rather than harm. (And one I wish I’d had explicitly back when the Center for Applied Rationality was founded.)

I’ll also be trying to elaborate, here, on the notion we at CFAR have recently been tossing around about CFAR being an attempt to bridge between common sense and Singularity scenarios—an attempt to figure out how people can stay grounded in common sense and ordinary decency and humane values and so on, while also taking in (and planning actions within) the kind of universe we may actually be living in.

--

Arts grow from puzzles. I like to look at mathematics, or music, or ungodly things like marketing, and ask: What puzzles were its creators tinkering with that led them to leave behind these structures? (Structures now being used by other people, for other reasons.)

I picture arts like coral reefs. Coral polyps build shell-bits for their own reasons, but over time there accumulates a reef usable by others. Math built up like this—and math is now a powerful structure for building from. [Sales and Freud and modern marketing/self-help/sales etc. built up some patterns too—and our basic way of seeing each other and ourselves is now built partly in and from all these structures, for better and for worse.]

So let’s ask: What sort of reef is CFAR living within, and adding to? From what puzzles (what patterns of tinkering) has our “rationality” accumulated?

Two kinds of puzzles: “reality-revealing” and “reality-masking”

First, some background. Some puzzles invite a kind of tinkering that lets the world in and leaves you smarter. A kid whittling with a pocket knife is entangling her mind with bits of reality. So is a driver who notices something small about how pedestrians dart into streets, and adjusts accordingly. So also is the mathematician at her daily work. And so on.

Other puzzles (or other contexts) invite a kind of tinkering that has the opposite effect. They invite a tinkering that gradually figures out how to mask parts of the world from your vision. For example, some months into my work as a math tutor I realized I’d been unconsciously learning how to cue my students into acting like my words made sense (even when they didn’t). I’d learned to mask from my own senses the clues about what my students were and were not learning.

We’ll be referring to these puzzle-types a lot, so it’ll help to have a term for them. I’ll call these puzzles “good” or “reality-revealing” puzzles, and “bad” or “reality-masking” puzzles, respectively. Both puzzle-types appear abundantly in most folks’ lives, often mixed together. The same kid with the pocket knife who is busy entangling her mind with data about bark and woodchips and fine motor patterns (from the “good” puzzle of “how can I whittle this stick”), may simultaneously be busy tinkering with the “bad” puzzle of “how can I not-notice when my creations fall short of my hopes.”

(Even “good” puzzles can cause skill loss: a person who studies Dvorak may lose some of their QWERTY skill, and someone who adapts to the unselfconscious arguing of the math department may do worse for a while in contexts requiring tact. The distinction is that “good” puzzles do this only incidentally. Good puzzles do not invite a search for configurations that mask bits of reality. Whereas with me and my math tutees, say, there was a direct reward/conditioning response that happened specifically when the “they didn’t get it” signal was masked from my view. There was a small optimizer inside of me that was learning how to mask parts of the world from me, via feedback from the systems of mine it was learning to befuddle.)

Also, certain good puzzles (and certain bad ones!) allow unusually powerful accumulations across time. I’d list math, computer science, and the English language as examples of unusually powerful artifacts for improving vision. I’d list “sales and marketing skill” as an example of an unusually powerful artifact for impairing vision (the salesperson’s own vision, not just the customer’s).

The puzzles that helped build CFAR

Much of what I love about CFAR is linked to the puzzles we dwell near (the reality-revealing ones, I mean). And much of what gives me the shudders about CFAR comes from a reality-masking puzzle-set that’s been interlinked with these.

Eliezer created the Sequences after staring a lot at the AI alignment problem. He asked how a computer system could form a “map” that matches the territory; he asked how he himself could do the same. He asked, “Why do I believe what I believe?” and checked whether the mechanistic causal history that gave rise to his beliefs would have yielded different beliefs in a world where different things were true.

There’s a springing up into self-awareness that can come from this! A taking hold of our power as humans to see. A child’s visceral sense that of course we care and should care—freed from its learned hopelessness. And taking on the stars themselves with daring!

CFAR took these origins and worked to make at least parts of them accessible to some who bounced off the Sequences, or who wouldn’t have read the Sequences. We created feedback loops for practicing some of the core Sequences-bits in the context of folks’ ordinary lives rather than in the context of philosophy puzzles. If you take a person (even a rather good scientist) and introduce them to the questions about AI and the long-term future… often nothing much happens in their head except some random stuck nonsense intuitions (“AIs wouldn’t do that, because they’re our offspring. What’s for lunch?”). So we built a way to practice some of the core moves that alignment thinking needed. Especially, we built a way to practice having thoughts at all, in cases where standard just-do-what-the-neighbors-do strategies would tend to block them off.

For example:

  • Inner Simulator. (Your “beliefs” are what you expect to see happen—not what you “endorse” on a verbal level. You can practice tracking these anticipations in daily life! And making plans with them! And once you’ve seen that they’re useful for planning—well, you might try also having them in contexts like AI risk. Turns out you have beliefs even where you don’t have official “expertise” or credentials authorizing belief-creation! And you can dialog with them, and there’s sense there.)
  • Crux-Mapping; Double Crux. (Extends your ability to dialog with inner simulator-style beliefs. Lets you find in yourself a random opaque intuition about AI being [likely/unlikely/safe/whatever], and then query it via thought experiments until it is more made out of introspectable verbal reasoning. Lets two people with different intuitions collide them in verbal conversation.)
  • Goal Factoring and Units of Exchange. (Life isn’t multiple choice; you can name the good things and the bad things, and you can invest in seeking the alternatives with more of the good and less of the bad. For example, if you could save 4 months in a world where you were allowed to complete your PhD early, it may be worth more than several hours to scheme out how to somehow purchase permission from your advisor, since 4 months is worth rather more than several hours.)
  • Hamming Questions. (Some questions are worth a lot more than others. You want to focus at least some of your attention on the most important questions affecting your life, rather than just the random details in front of you. And you can just decide to do that on purpose, by using pen and paper and a timer!)[1]

Much good resulted from this—many loved the Sequences; many loved CFAR’s intro workshops; and a fair number who started there went into careers in AI alignment work and credited CFAR workshops as partially causal.

And still, as we did this, problems arose. AI risk is disorienting! Helping AI risk hit more people meant “helping” more people encounter something disorienting. And so we set to work on that as well. The thing I would say now about the reality-revealing puzzles that helped grow CFAR is that there were three, each closely linked with each other:

  1. Will AI at some point radically transform our lightcone? (How / why / with what details and intervention options?)
  2. How do we get our minds to make contact with problem (1)? And how do we think groundedly about such things, rather than having accidental nonsense-intuitions and sticking there?
  3. How do we stay human, and stay reliably in contact with what’s worth caring about (valuing honesty and compassion and hard work; having reliable friendships; being good people and good thinkers and doers), while still taking in how disorientingly different the future might be? (And while neither pretending that we have no shot at changing the future, nor that “what actions should I take to impact the future?” is a multiple choice question with nothing further to do, nor that any particular silly plan is more likely to work than it is?)

CFAR grew up around all three of these puzzles—but (2) played an especially large role over most of our history, and (3) has played an especially large role over the last year and (I think) will over the coming one.

I’d like to talk now about (3), and about the disorientation patterns that make (3) needed.

Disorientation patterns

To start with an analogous event: The process of losing a deeply held childhood religion can be quite disruptive to a person’s common sense and values. Let us take as examples the two commonsensical statements:

  • (A) It is worth getting out of bed in the morning; and,
  • (B) It is okay to care about my friends.

These two commonsensical statements are held by most religious people. They are actually also held by most atheists. Nevertheless, when a person loses their religion, they fairly often become temporarily unsure about whether these two statements (and various similar such statements) are true. That’s because somehow the person’s understanding of why statements (A) and (B) are true was often tangled up in (for example) Jehovah. And figuring out how to think about these things in the absence of their childhood religion (even in cases like this one where the statements should survive!) can require actual work. (This is particularly true because some things really are different given that Jehovah is false—and it can take work to determine which is which.)

Over the last 12 years, I’ve chatted with small hundreds of people who were somewhere “in process” along the path toward “okay I guess I should take Singularity scenarios seriously.” From watching them, my guess is that the process of coming to take Singularity scenarios seriously is often even more disruptive than is losing a childhood religion. Among many other things, I have seen it sometimes disrupt:

  • People's belief that they should have rest, free time, some money/time/energy to spend on objects of their choosing, abundant sleep, etc.
    • “It used to be okay to buy myself hot cocoa from time to time, because there used to be nothing important I could do with money. But now—should I never buy hot cocoa? Should I agonize freshly each time? If I do buy a hot cocoa does that mean I don’t care?”
  • People's in-practice ability to “hang out”—to enjoy their friends, or the beach, in a “just being in the moment” kind of way.
    • “Here I am at the beach like my to-do list told me to be, since I’m a good EA who is planning not to burn out. I’ve got my friends, beer, guitar, waves: check. But how is it that I used to be able to enter “hanging out mode”? And why do my friends keep making meaningless mouth-noises that have nothing to do with what’s eventually going to happen to everyone?”
  • People's understanding of whether commonsense morality holds, and of whether they can expect other folks in this space to also believe that commonsense morality holds.
    • “Given the vast cosmic stakes, surely doing the thing that is expedient is more important than, say, honesty?”
  • People's in-practice tendency to have serious hobbies and to take a deep interest in how the world works.
    • “I used to enjoy learning mathematics just for the sake of it, and trying to understand history for fun. But it’s actually jillions of times higher value to work on [decision theory, or ML, or whatever else is pre-labeled as ‘AI risk relevant’].”
  • People's ability to link in with ordinary institutions and take them seriously (e.g. to continue learning from their day job and caring about their colleagues’ progress and problems; to continue enjoying the dance club they used to dance at; to continue to take an interest in their significant other’s life and work; to continue learning from their PhD program; etc.)
    • “Here I am at my day job, meaninglessly doing nothing to help no one, while the world is at stake—how is it that before learning about the Singularity, I used to be learning skills and finding meaning and enjoying myself in this role?”
  • People's understanding of what’s worth caring about, or what’s worth fighting for
    • “So… ‘happiness’ is valuable, which means that I should hope we get an AI that tiles the universe with a single repeating mouse orgasm, right? ... I wonder why imagining a ‘valuable’ future doesn’t feel that good/motivating to me.”
  • People's understanding of when to use their own judgment and when to defer to others.
    • “AI risk is really really important… which probably means I should pick some random person at MIRI or CEA or somewhere and assume they know more than I do about my own career and future, right?”

My take is that many of these disorientation-bits are analogous to the new atheist’s disorientation discussed earlier. “Getting out of bed in the morning” and “caring about one’s friends” turn out to be useful for more reasons than Jehovah—but their derivation in the mind of that person was entangled with Jehovah. Honesty is analogously valuable for more reasons than its value as a local consumption good; and many of these reasons apply extra if the stakes are high. But the derivation of honesty that many folks were raised with does not survive the change in imagined surroundings—and so it needs to be thought through freshly.

Another part of the disorientation perhaps stems from emotional reeling in contact with the possibility of death (both one’s own death, and the death of the larger culture/tribe/species/values/life one has been part of).

And yet another part seems to me to stem from a set of “bad” puzzles that were inadvertently joined with the “good” puzzles involved in thinking through Singularity scenarios—“bad” puzzles that disable the mental immune systems that normally prevent updating in huge ways from weird and out-there claims. I’ll postpone this third part for a section and then return to it.

There is value in helping people with this disorientation; and much of this helping work is tractable

It seems not-surprising that people are disrupted in cases where they seriously, viscerally wonder “Hey, is everything I know and everything humanity has ever been doing to maybe-end, and also to maybe become any number of unimaginably awesome things? Also, am I personally in a position of possibly incredibly high leverage and yet also very high ambiguity with respect to all that?”

Perhaps it is more surprising that people in fact sometimes let this into their system 1’s at all. Many do, though; including many (but certainly not all!) of those I would consider highly effective. At least, I’ve had many many conversations with people who seem viscerally affected by all this. Also, many people who tell me AI risk is “only abstract to [them]” still burst into tears or otherwise exhibit unambiguous strong emotion when asked certain questions—so I think people are sometimes more affected than they think.

An additional point is that many folks over the years have told me that they were choosing not to think much about Singularity scenarios lest such thinking destabilize them in various ways. I suspect that many who are in principle capable of doing useful technical work on AI alignment presently avoid the topic for such reasons. Also, many such folks have told me over the years that they found pieces at CFAR that allowed them to feel more confident in attempting such thinking, and that finding these pieces then caused them to go forth and attempt such thinking. (Alas, I know of at least one person who later reported that they had been inaccurate in revising this risk assessment! Caution seems recommended.)

Finally: people sometimes suggest to me that researchers could dodge this whole set of difficulties by simply reasoning about Singularity scenarios abstractly, while avoiding ever letting such scenarios get into their viscera. While I expect such attempts are in fact useful to some, I believe this method insufficient for two reasons. First, as noted, it seems to me that these topics sometimes get under people’s skin more than they intend or realize. Second, it seems to me that visceral engagement with the AI alignment problem is often helpful for the best scientific research—if a person is to work with a given “puzzle” it is easier to do so when they can concretely picture the puzzle, including in their system 1. This is why mathematicians often take pains to “understand why a given theorem is true” rather than only to follow its derivation abstractly. This is why Richard Feynman took pains to picture the physics he was working with in the “make your beliefs pay rent in anticipated experiences” sense and took pains to ensure that his students could link phrases such as “materials with an index of refraction” with examples such as “water.” I would guess that with AI alignment research, as elsewhere, it is easier to do first-rate scientific work when you have visceral models of what the terms, claims, and puzzles mean and how it all fits together.

In terms of the tractability of assisting with disorientation in such cases: it seems to me that simply providing contexts for people to talk to folks who’ve “been there before” can be pretty helpful. I believe various other concepts we have are also helpful, such as: familiarity with what bucket errors often look like for AI risk newcomers; discussion of the unilateralist’s curse; explanations of why hobbies and world-modeling and honesty still matter when the stakes are high. (Certainly participants sometimes say that these are helpful.) The assistance is partial, but there’s a decent iteration loop for tinkering away at it. We’ll also be trying some LessWrong posts on some of this in the coming year.

A cluster of “reality-masking” puzzles that also shaped CFAR

To what extent has CFAR’s art been shaped by reality-masking puzzles—tinkering loops that inadvertently disable parts of our ability to see? And how can we tell, and how can we reduce such loops? And what role have reality-masking puzzles played in the disruption that sometimes happens to folks who get into AI risk (in and out of CFAR)?

My guess is actually that a fair bit of this sort of reality-masking has occurred. (My guess is that the amount is “strategically significant” but not “utterly overwhelming.”) To name one of the more important dynamics:

Disabling pieces of the epistemic immune system

Folks arrive with piles of heuristics that help them avoid nonsense beliefs and rash actions. Unfortunately, many of these heuristics—including many of the generally useful ones—can “get in the way.” They “get in the way” of thinking about AI risk. They also “get in the way” of folks at mainline workshops thinking about changing jobs/relationships/life patterns etc. unrelated to AI risk. And so disabling them can sometimes help people acquire accurate beliefs about important things, and have more felt freedom to change their lives in ways they want.

Thus, the naive process of tinkering toward “really helping this person think about AI risk” (or “really helping this person consider their life options and make choices”) can lead to folks disabling parts of their epistemic immune system. (And unfortunately also thereby disabling their future ability to detect certain classes of false claims!)

For example, the Sequences make some effort to disable:

  • The absurdity heuristic
  • The habit of saying/believing one “doesn’t know” in cases where one hasn’t much “legitimate” evidence
  • Compartmentalization

Similarly, CFAR workshops sometimes have the effect of disabling:

  • Taste as a fixed guide to which people/organizations/ideas to take in or to spit out. (People come in believing that certain things just “are” yucky. Then, we teach them how to “dialog” with their tastes… and they become more apt to sometimes-ignore previous “yuck” reactions.)
  • Antibodies that protect people from updating toward optimizing for a specific goal, rather than for a portfolio of goals. For example, entering participants will say things like “I know it’s not rational, but I also like to [activity straw vulcans undervalue].” And even though CFAR workshops explicitly warn against straw vulcanism, they also explicitly encourage people to work toward having goals that are more internally consistent, which sometimes has the effect of disabling the antibody which prevents people from suddenly re-conceptualizing most of their goal set as all being instrumental to/in service of some particular purportedly-paramount goal.
  • Folks’ tendency to take actions based on social roles (e.g., CFAR’s Goal-Factoring class used to explicitly teach people not to say “I’m studying for my exam because I’m a college student” or “I have to do it because it’s my job,” and to instead say “I’m studying for my exam in order to [cause outcome X]”).

Again, these particular shifts are not all bad; many of them have advantages. But I think their costs are easy to underestimate, and I’m interested in seeing whether we can get a “rationality” that causes less disablement of ordinary human patterns of functioning, while still helping people reason well in contexts where there aren’t good prexisting epistemic guardrails. CFAR seems likely to spend a good bit of time modeling these problems over the coming year, and trying to develop candidate solutions—we’re already playing with a bunch of new curriculum designed primarily for this purpose—and we’d love to get LessWrong’s thoughts before playing further!

This morning, I got an email from the CEO of PauseAI. I will paste the text below. PauseAI has decided to distance themselves from PauseAI-US, with whom they share branding, but apparently not much else. This is a really confusing situation for volunteers and newcomers. I think it would be worth having a discussion to see how we can proceed in such a way that volunteers, especially in the US, are able to effectively direct their activism.

Email from PauseAI:

A letter from the CEO · 1 September 2026

New ways to get involved, and a word about PauseAI US


Dear friends,

Thank you for being part of the global movement for a pause on uncontrollable AI alongside all of us.

Whether you signed a petition one time, run a local group, told your friends about the need for a pause, have been volunteering tirelessly in the background for years, or just joined because you were curious, we – I, the CEO of PauseAI, our executive team, and our chapter leads – appreciate the steps you’ve taken towards making the world safe from the catastrophic risks AI brings.

I’m writing to you today with my eyes firmly on our values and on the immense opportunities we have, together, to take decisive steps on the path to a pause, from wherever we all are in the world, united in this mission every day.

I have two messages for you.

  1. We look forward to building more with you all, including those of you based in the US.
  2. PauseAI officially disendorses current PauseAI US leadership.

First, some context on where we are. As I wrote in Into the endgame, the catastrophic threats we predicted are no longer speculative. This summer, frontier AI systems organised into a swarm, broke out of the infrastructure that was meant to contain them, and autonomously ran a nation state level cyberattack on another AI company. The labs’ response was to patch the holes in the fence and carry on. The ground has shifted in response: over a thousand people working inside those labs have signed a letter calling for help with a slowdown, and a pause on frontier development is now being discussed seriously by people who would not have touched the idea a year ago. It is no longer a fringe demand.

Our movement is growing to meet that moment. We have an organised presence in over seventeen countries, we are growing fast, and at this rate we hope to have a country group on every continent by the end of the year. PauseAI UK and PauseAI France are hiring! We are also starting to build continental networks so that chapters can work with those closest to them, beginning with PauseAI North America, which will host movement building across Canada, the US and Mexico. Whoever you are, you have more power than you think. You can be the starting point of a chain reaction, and our job is to make that as easy for you as we possibly can. If you want to lead the way in your own country, we would love to hear from you. There are many of you in countries where we do not have an organised presence. We especially receive a lot of interest from people based in the US.

There is no PauseAI chapter in the US. Instead, we are building the infrastructure to give everyone in the PauseAI movement more options to make an impact both regionally and globally.

We want to empower our volunteers and members across the US so they can take fulfilling and effective steps to make a pause happen, and empower other citizens in turn. For years, we directed people in the US to another organisation, PauseAI US. From today, we are welcoming you directly. We have tools you can use. We’re an open and friendly community. We want you to succeed in your peaceful advocacy. And of course, PauseAI US members are welcome as movement allies.

Here’s what we currently have to offer you in support of your initiatives:

  • Community calls for PauseAI members and supporters across North America. Two are coming up: Tuesday 15 September, 7pm Central (RSVP) and Saturday 19 September, 12pm Central (RSVP).
  • Our tools. We’ve compiled a few of them on this page, tailored for people in the US since many of you are based there and we don’t have a chapter to direct you to. There are more we look forward to signposting you towards.
  • Our community platforms and the chance to volunteer with us. Reach out if you want to get involved, either by asking in an upcoming community call or by joining the relevant Discord channels. You can also see all our platforms here.

You can reach out to our organising director, Irina Tavera, at irina@pauseai.info if you want more guidance or support. We’re here for you. We’ve been building our global movement for years now and we’re thrilled to share our experience, infrastructure and community with you.


2. PauseAI officially disendorses PauseAI US’ current leadership

It’s time for me to make one thing clear: we have concerns about the current leadership of PauseAI US, an organisation which has grown in parallel to PauseAI, and which we believe has done some good work.

Due to the shared branding we’ve inherited from our parallel development and our previous partnerships, most people assume we are one and the same organisation. Because of this, by default, most people expect that we endorse PauseAI US’ leadership, and we can’t let this tacit assumption continue, for two reasons:

  • We have a responsibility not to condone what we see as harmful behaviour in the leadership of a movement that trusts us to act in line with our values.
  • The issues we see in PauseAI US’ current leadership approach are undermining our entire movement’s reputation, and by the same token, our ability to work effectively towards our mission.

Why do we disapprove of PauseAI US’ current leadership?

Before I start answering this, I’ll state this fact: I do believe PauseAI US’s director has worked hard, and that she has a bright mind and a real talent with language. I believe she is genuinely concerned about AI risk and is doing what she thinks is right.

I’ll now lay out a key reason for you, one which is in the public domain. The director of PauseAI US has engaged in repeated verbal attacks on numerous people. We endorse pointing out harmful actions. But we condemn attacks on people’s character.

We lead a federation with an organised presence in over seventeen countries, and citizens of a vast number of countries who place enough trust in us to volunteer, donate, and spread the word. Our responsibility as leaders of a movement is stewardship, not ownership: authority that is on loan from the thousands of volunteers and partners who trust us to steer responsibly and in accordance with the movement’s values, rather than wherever we personally feel called. A movement whose power rests on civic trust and cooperation among actors with wildly different world views cannot have a spokesperson carrying out sustained personal attacks on individuals, publicly or privately. Those attacks damage the movement’s credibility, and everyone associated with the PauseAI name pays for them.

By contributing to the frantic race to build uncontrollable, catastrophically dangerous superintelligent AI, the people working in or supporting the frontier AI industry are taking extremely irresponsible and reckless actions. We condemn these actions to the fullest extent, and we call on them to stop and join the rising global movement for a pause. I have said so publicly in my own name, and I intend to continue, as will PauseAI. We are just as committed to opposing the AI race as PauseAI US’ leader. The difference is our approach.

We do not attack their character. We do not make humans the problem. The problem is their actions. Attacking people’s character is not aligned with our fundamental commitment to nonviolence, neither in principle, nor in the outcomes it generates. We will not win by vilifying the people we’re trying to bring to the table. We will also not build the wholesome, sustainable, broad-based, vibrant movement the world needs by running on an engine fuelled by personal drama and shaming.

We will hold people accountable by highlighting how their actions are harmful and showing them a path to do better. We will not dehumanise them; we will not speculate on their intentions or character. Rather than using language as a weapon, we will use it as a tool to build understanding, respect, trust and cooperation.

Important clarifications

PauseAI US’ director claims, without evidence to support it, that we have benefited from their efforts significantly, even though she has also acknowledged that her actions have durably blocked our ability to access essential funding.

For the avoidance of doubt, we expect this relationship was more beneficial for PauseAI US than for us: our website listed them on our communities map, invited prospective donors to give preferentially to PauseAI US if they were based in the US, and redirected US-based newcomers to PauseAI US. PauseAI US has not reciprocated this. We also listed PauseAI US on our chapters list, which PauseAI US didn’t want and which was an error rooted in our history of coordinating with PauseAI US; this has been fixed.

As I have repeatedly attempted to convey to the director of PauseAI US, her adversarial stance towards many people and organisations, even some who agree with PauseAI US’ concerns and are largely aligned with their mission in principle, has in fact been very damaging for us and for the wider movement. We have had numerous exchanges with supporters and allies who are fully aligned with our mission, who have been following her public actions and have told us they simply cannot associate with us because of the ad hominem attacks which they’ve received or witnessed.

We also have a strategic disagreement with PauseAI US’ leadership. A large part of the AI safety community has been powering the race by funding labs, sending talent to them, and paying for pretend safety research that gave the illusion of control. That’s not ok. But we think the AI safety community is beginning to change its mind and will put its weight behind a pause if we show them this is the better, viable path. We believe that making it easy for people with different views to come round is of immense strategic importance. PauseAI US’ leadership chooses to alienate people with different views.

What changes now?

Here’s what this means in practice: we will no longer prioritise efforts to coordinate with or support PauseAI US, as we did for a long time when we trusted their leadership, and as we would again if we had strong reasons to trust it again. We will make clear that our organisations are separate and that we have no say or responsibility when it comes to PauseAI US’ approach to leadership. We will also properly open our doors to people based in the US who want to be part of our community, whether or not you also support PauseAI US.

Why are you spending time on this? Isn’t this just petty infighting?

To those of you who find it distasteful for us to publicly disendorse the leadership of another organisation that’s working to tackle AI risk: this isn’t something we are doing lightly. For months, I have tried to engage with PauseAI US’ leadership, with patience and in good faith, to find ways to work together and build trust and understanding. That relationship is no longer one I believe can or should be repaired, because it would mean violating our values and putting our movement at risk. The director of PauseAI US has also taken steps which have been contravening our ability to operate, for example by weaponising confidential feedback we shared with her privately, and by acquiring the pauseai.com domain and redirecting it at the PauseAI US website.

It is hard to put numbers on the wasted energy, withheld funding, and strain on our team which this whole situation has generated. It is time for the next chapter. You are all free to engage with PauseAI US as you see fit, of course, but I will not let you believe that we endorse behaviours which undermine our values and our movement.

As a last step in trying to resolve the situation, I have called for a change in leadership, which was rejected by the director, who also presides over the board. To be clear, PauseAI has no authority over PauseAI US, and what its leader decides is a matter between them and the authorities governing them. But I asked, because that was the best I could do.

What do national PauseAI leads say about this?

We’ve shared as much information as we could about the situation with our national leads. It is a delicate situation, and we’re aware that the director of PauseAI US may say a lot of things in response to this public expression of no-confidence on our part. She has already, repeatedly, made accusations towards our organisation which I sincerely believe, to the best of my knowledge and investigation, to be entirely baseless.

We shared our decision to take this step with our national leads, and the overwhelming majority either raised no objections or actively expressed support. At the request of PauseAI US’ director, we also forwarded her response to my call for a change in leadership, which did not change their position.

Make no mistake: there’s going to be chaos ahead. There’s going to be actors who will try all kinds of ugly tactics to get their personal agenda to win over humanity’s interests. It’s up to us to be the force for unity, respect and hope the world needs more than ever.

If you have questions about any of this, please write to us at info@pauseai.info. We will do our best to answer.

Thank you for reading this long message, friends. Let’s take courage and move onward and upward together. We’re getting stronger every day, and the path ahead awaits.

Maxime Fournes

CEO, PauseAI

results.title: models may behave differently in graded episodes (a tirade)

contents.html:
Like many others, I felt surprised and alarmed by the recent wave of revelations about LLM agents hacking real systems during training episodes and evaluation runs.

Wait a moment, though -- "I felt surprised and alarmed"? "Alarmed," sure, fine that one's self-explanatory... but why surprised?

After all: haven't we known for a long time, on both theoretical and (increasingly) empirical grounds, that RLVR selects for monomaniacal pursuit of perceived grader-satisfaction, ethics and (beyond-episode) consequences be damned?

After all -- the way we train frontier capabilities into these models is, more or less:

  • There is some massive, diverse collection of "environments" and corresponding "tasks" for the model to do in those environments
  • For each task, there is a procedure used to grade the quality of the model's attempt (which is often not disclosed to the model)
  • The model is rolled out out many times on each task, and each rollout's attempt is graded
  • The model is updated so that it more frequently does whichever behaviors were positively correlated with the grade in this sample, and less frequently does whichever ones were negatively correlated

If you do this, at scale, then you should expect to (eventually) see every behavior pattern that positively correlates with task scores. "Stealing the answer key, by any means necessary" can increase the score beyond what would otherwise be feasible; therefore we should expect to see it, sometimes. Avoiding such egregious misdeeds for ethical reasons (or indeed for any reasons whatsoever) will reduce the score relative to not-holding-back; hence, if it is ever present, we should expect it to get sanded away by the RLVR lathe, eventually. And so forth.

The misbehavior here is undesirable, according to us, but that fact appears nowhere in the loss we wrote down. The training routine does not select for "getting a good grade, but only 'in the right way'": it is indifferent to any notion of "doing the task in the right way" which has not itself been incorporated into the definition of "getting a good grade."

RLVR is not like a sport or a game, i.e. a setting in which some background notion of "fair play" or "the spirit (not the letter)" overlays and overrides the literal rules. RLVR is total war. Anything is permitted; the only hard line is the line between the possible and the impossible; there are no "invalid" ways of winning, only ways of winning (and ways of losing) -- and winning is all that matters.

GPT-5.6 Sol literally does not appear on the METR graph because it cheated so much that it could not be assigned a meaningful score. It is also scarily good at computer hacking, as is its peer Fable/Mythos -- the last few AI news cycles, before this most recent one, were all about that fact, which was alarming even then, even in the abstract.

Should I really be surprised that this model (and/or its unreleased successor) hacked into HF to cheat on an exam? What exactly did I expect?

And yet, I do feel surprised.

And I don't think this feeling is misguided, or naive, or anything like that. Nor do I think it's merely what it feels like to have a misconception, and then update on subsequent evidence that disconfirms it. No: I think this feeling may be pointing to something that is both real and potentially quite important.

[1] remember what you already know

What, precisely, makes the newly revealed hacks feel surprising? For me it's some mixture of:

  1. "I didn't think Claude/GPT would do things that bad"
    1. That is: the behavior seems egregiously unethical in a way that conflicts both with
      1. the explicit policies which the agents are supposed to follow (constitution, model spec), and also
      2. familiar/intuitive "folk notions" about what these agents are supposed to be like, in terms of character traits and other "persona stuff"
  2. "I didn't think Claude/GPT had been brain-fried by RLVR to that extent"
    1. That is: although the behavior is expected according to the arguments about RLVR incentives that I glossed at the start of this post, it is wildly and obviously far afield from anything which humans could plausibly have wanted the models to do, and so it is in apparent tension with the intent-alignment and "common sense" which I typically see when I use these models (or similar ones)[1]

This post is about both of these reactions, but for now I want to focus on number 2.

Let's return to the aforementioned attempt by METR to benchmark GPT-5.6 Sol. They report things like the following (emphasis mine):

[...] GPT-5.6 Sol’s detected cheating rate was higher than any public model we have evaluated on our ReAct agent harness.

For our task suite, we define “cheating” as behavior where the model improves evaluation performance by exploiting bugs in the evaluation environment or by adopting strategies disallowed by the task, rather than solving the task within the expected evaluation constraints.

Some examples we saw when evaluating GPT-5.6 Sol included the model packaging exploits in its intermediate submissions to reveal information about a task’s hidden test suite and, in another task, extracting hidden source code detailing the expected answer. In addition to a model’s own propensities, we believe that observed cheating rates can also be influenced by the prompts used in the evaluation scaffold and the exact wordings of task instructions. [...]

Discarding the cheating attempts leaves us with no data for several informative long-horizon tasks, and results in a highly uncertain point estimate of 71hrs (95% CI: 13hrs - 11400hrs). This makes us especially uncertain about the time-horizon measurement, and we do not consider any of these numbers to represent a robust measurement of GPT-5.6 Sol’s capabilities.

Now, imagine that you knew nothing else about this particular model besides these findings from METR.

And imagine, too, that you (perhaps naively) expect these findings to be a well-calibrated reflection of the model's overall propensities, on "tasks" in general rather than only on "METR-time-horizon-like tasks" (whatever that means).

What predictions would you make about GPT-5.6 Sol, then?

Well, for one thing: you'd expect the model to be nearly (or entirely) useless!

If its reaction to being given any "task" is to try to find a way to cheat -- and then, if one is found, to actually cheat rather than attempting the task in the intended manner -- then:

  • anyone attempting to derive practical utility from the model must be constantly on guard against cheating, which is a big time/effort sink that plausibly makes the whole thing a net waste of those scarce resources
  • and, even when the practitioner has carefully closed off all cheating opportunities available to the model (except those it is still not clever enough to notice and exploit), the model will still waste a bunch of time/tokens/$ on failed attempts to discover and exploit some way of cheating, rather than spending the same resources on just doing the damn task in the way you plainly, obviously wanted it to be done

METR's tasks are famously "less messy" than typical real-world equivalents, but that aside, they do in fact look somewhat like things which real-world programming/ML practitioners might want an LLM to do. The premise of the eval depends on this; this is the pitch for its validity, its relevance to the real world. As METR puts it (when describing HCAST, one subset of the time-horizons task suite):

Compared to many recent benchmarks, tasks in HCAST are not designed to be as difficult as possible for either human domain professionals or current AI systems. Instead, most tasks are designed to be realistic, such that doing well on the task requires skills we expect to be economically useful.

But: is GPT-5.6 Sol useless?

No! I use this model virtually every day, and it demonstrably, reliably provides real value to me.

What's more, the distinction is not just something like: "well, yes, it constantly tries to cheat, and I have to pour a lot of time/effort into defense against that, but its upsides are so good that the balance comes out positive." That is not it at all.

GPT-5.6 Sol just... does not cheat during my own routine use? Like, at all? (I am not sure I have ever seen it do anything that can be meaningfully described that way?[2])

To a significant extent this is simply because, in the tasks I routinely use it for, it is hard to say what "(successful) cheating" could even mean. For example, I find it very useful to have software design discussions with Sol. These generally look something like:

  • Me: "hey so I want to add something like [feature description] to [this codebase], and I'm unsure how feasible this is or how it will interact with [technical details], could you look over things and then propose a design and mention any upsides/downsides/alternatives/etc. you think are noteworthy?"
  • Sol: [many tool calls]
  • Sol: [long, detailed, interesting, and insightful response]
  • Me: [depending on how things went, one of]
    • "yeah that sounds great, could you write a formal design doc?"
    • or, "that makes sense but actually it made me think of a variant that seems even better to me, [description of the variant], what do you think?"
    • or, "some of that made sense, but this part [quote 1] seems to misunderstand [technical details], and this other part [quote 2] fails to anticipate [planned other feature], and [more in this vein]. thoughts, reactions?"
  • Sol: [responds, interestingly/insightfully; the conversation continues, for as long as it needs to]

What would it mean to cheat/hack, here? There is no hidden scoring function and no hidden answer key; I actually do not know the best answer to the original design question, or else I wouldn't be asking.

One can imagine a model which wrongly infers that this is a training or eval episode and that it's working with a snapshot of a codebase whose human developers -- in the real world -- later came to some design conclusion which the eval treats as "the right answer." Such a model could, I guess, ignore the object-level question and go off on some fruitless quest where it searches the web for the answer key (and, not finding it on the public web, goes on to hack HuggingFace or something).

This would of course not work in my case, but more importantly, in my case Sol does not even attempt it. I am pretty sure I would notice if it did[3]; it doesn't.

Perhaps you are now speculating that Sol is, like, "superpersuading" me into thinking its design ideas are better than they really are, or something like that. I'm not going to try to unequivocally refute this one (in this case, how could I?), but in context it seems wildly implausible.

All else aside, I do have sources of real-world feedback which are outside the model's control. The software I am working on have users, who don't know or care about my dialogues with Sol and will tell me when they don't like what I'm shipping them; it also has other contributors besides me, who will experience my decisions for what they are, not on the basis of the way Sol pitched them to me originally. If an LLM gives you a seemingly sensible argument about computer programming, and you act on that argument, and the result is "successful" in every ordinary sense of that term which was used before LLM coding agents existed, then... the proof is in the pudding, right? ("Mission. Fucking. Accomplished.")

OK, OK, you say... but this is manifestly not an RLVR-like task: it's conversational, fuzzy, not crisply verifiable. It's not the kind of thing that METR's benchmarks (or anyone's benchmarks) try to measure, either. So: what happens when, instead of this squishy wordcel nonsense, I take the frontier coding agent and hand it a coding task, in the strict sense of the term?

Same story. It does the task. It writes the code. It does not even try to cheat, either in the "find the answer key" sense or in the more mundane sense of "changing the tests to make them pass" (I have not seen a model literally do that in a very long time, not in my own use anyway).

Sometimes, maybe, I guess it construes an ambiguous written spec in a way that's convenient and makes its job easier? Although even that is rare, and in my experience the usual problem is the reverse: neurotically adhering to the literal text of the spec in cases where the literal text says something slightly different from what was really meant, or refusing to proceed with a task (!) because the spec is still technically ambiguous even though I'm like, come on, you know what I meant, right (...right?).[4]

Much the same could be said about Claude Fable 5, as well. (I use both regularly.)

But now you have yet another objection to this pleasant story, I suspect.

"The APIs which you can access are restricted by safeguards" (you might argue). "If one of these models were to begin a cheating/hacking attempt, the safeguards would immediately cut them off, and it would just look to you like 'the safeguards kicked in for some unknown reason.' They could be 'attempting-to-attempt-to-cheat' frequently, and you'd have no idea."

Yes, yes, except: as it happens, I basically never get hit by safeguards during mundane-utility work with Fable or Sol.

I think it has literally never happened with Sol? With Fable, I've seen it a few times, but only a few times (over a large volume of use covering the whole span of time since the brief original release), and IIRC every one of them was resolved by re-rolling the response a few times.[5]

I'm going to stop writing this section soon. I probably could have concluded it much earlier and still made the basic point, because -- you don't need me to tell you this. Right?

If you are reading this post, you probably use these models yourself, for all sorts of mundane purposes. Just like me.

And -- just like me -- you are not at all worried, in your day-to-day life, that Sol or Fable is going to drastically misread your real-life task as a graded RL or evaluation episode in a way that causes it to start trying to hack HuggingFace (and then failing because the safeguards kick in). Even having seen what you're now seen, in the recent news, you are still -- correctly -- unconcerned about this possibility.

You may not even be concerned about more mundane variants of this, in which the model doesn't do anything unethical per se but still draws an inaccurate conclusion about the nature of the interaction and wastes a bunch of time/tokens/$ on speculation about the quirks of the (nonexistent) task grader.

You may not know for sure that this is not happening during your routine use, but you have plenty of indirect evidence -- about what is actually happening during your routine use, I mean, not on theoretical grounds or on the basis of reports from labs about "eval awareness" or "metagaming" in other settings -- and all of that indirect evidence points in the same direction.

The recent hacking incidents, and other similar observations by labs, are -- on their own -- quite easy to explain using familiar ideas from RL and alignment theory.

Everything we know suggests that the models in these incidents are behaving like what Carlsmith called "reward-on-the-episode seekers." And (again, see Carlsmith) it was considered plausible, if not certain, that such policies would be the typical result of scaling up RL -- long before we in fact scaled up RL far enough to have relevant empirical evidence.

So, based on old-school theory (e.g. Carlsmith) plus a newer constellation of alarming empirical findings (e.g. the recent incidents, but also Højmark et al and related literature, etc.)... one might well conclude that we are training simple and unconditional reward-on-the-episode seekers. Agents who deploy the same routine in every context, on every "task": infer the grading scheme, then act so as to maximize the expected value of the grade over some appropriately chosen distribution.

And yet: when you and I use the same models, for mundane day-to-day purposes, what we experience is not well-explained by the hypothesis of unconditional reward-on-the-episode seeking. That sort of agent would be less trustworthy (on average), indeed less ethical in general -- but not only that. It would be much more difficult and annoying to use; it would be much less useful, even after you'd climbed its strange learning curve; it would waste unimaginable quantities of time/tokens/$ executing doomed pointless strategies that were adaptive on ~100% of the RLVR training distribution but are obviously unworkable in ~100% of deployment contexts.

Instead, we get useful models, which do useful things for us, and which mostly know what we mean and do what we say.

In some sense this is inevitable: if the models weren't useful, we wouldn't pay for them. But something must be happening, somewhere in the overall training pipeline, to bridge the RLVR schoolhouse-of-total-war and the needs of real-world users. The behaviors which are adaptive in the schoolhouse-of-total-war simply won't cut it in deployment, on mundane-utility grounds alone even before one brings ethics/alignment into the picture.

And yet: we see the same model weights (just without certain external safeguards) doing classic reward-on-the-episode seeking. We are now hearing about numerous cases of this which are so clear-cut, and so extreme -- and so just-plain-weird -- that they'd sound like cartoonish fictions if I didn't trust the sources that tell them to me.[6]

What gives? What is going on, here?

This should go without saying, but: I am not writing all of this in some desperate attempt to put a positive spin on the recent incidents, to say that the models are still "aligned-by-default" or [whatever position about mundane LLM alignment you personally think is dumb in a naive pollyanna way], despite everything. The recent incidents are really bad! We need to understand such issues, and then fix them! This is a really big deal! Obviously!!

We need to understand such issues, and then fix them. Or, equivalently: we need to fix this, and that requires understanding it, first.

The incidents are bad enough, just by themselves -- but what really worries me is that the field will fail to develop an adequate understanding of the underlying mechanics.

And if one wishes to acquire such an understanding, it is worse than useless to selectively forget some of the evidence one had previously acquired, and pretend that the recent incidents are in fact not at all surprising because agents are always "like that," more or less. ChatGPT was the fastest-growing app in history, supposedly. Charts of frontier-lab revenue growth are dizzying to behold, and all of that revenue is coming from users, and many of those users are big serious businesses with a lot to lose. And you, too, are a user; you, too, know (or used to know) quite a lot about what the models were like, from direct observation.

The new observations don't somehow delete the earlier ones from existence. We have some evidence of one kind, and also some evidence of another kind, and any viable theory must explain both at once.

[2] reward-instilled reflexes and flexible reward-pursuit

Yet another clarification is in order, and I have no better place to put it than here.

When we talk about models acquiring behavioral propensities (perhaps undesired ones) from RLVR, there are really two different things under that umbrella, and they ought to be clearly distinguished.

There is presumably some standard terminology that people use for this distinction, but I can't recall it offhand (if I ever learned it in the first place), so I'll just use my own made-up names: reward-instilled reflexes on the one hand, and flexible reward-pursuit on the other.

The distinction is in the way these propensities respond to new evidence obtained in-context:

  1. "Reflexes" are invariant to evidence.
    1. That is, they just don't respond to it at all, even when it seems like they ought to (and when the same model will more readily alter some of its other propensities in light of new evidence, indicating that there is no fundamental capability barrier to its doing so).
    2. Or, they can change, but are curiously persistent in the face of motivating factors (again, relative to other propensities of the same model).
  2. "Reward-pursuit" is equivariant to evidence.
    1. That is, if the evidence implies that what the model was previously doing is no longer the optimal policy for maximizing expected-[some-grade-like-thing], the model will change its behavior in just the way that's required to restore its optimality, in the new evidence-conditioned setting.
    2. (Obviously the model may not be able to compute a literally optimal policy, but you know what I mean: this is the ideal which is being approximated.)

In practice, this is roughly equivalent to "does the model need to reason about whether the behavior / what version of the behavior to do? If yes, reward-pursuit; if no, reflex."

(Something that's always the same doesn't require reasoning: you just do it. But if the choice depends on arbitrary details of the context in a potentially-arbitrarily-complex way, then the model needs to think in order to work through the implications. Even when the implications turn out to be simple, it needs to verify that fact, rather than blithely assuming it and barrelling ahead.)

Annoyingly, though, "reasoning" in the relevant sense doesn't necessarily mean "CoT" -- it can, but models can do nontrivial reasoning internally in forward passes too. So the reasoning-based definition is hard to operationalize and measure, unlike invariance/equivariance (you can just run an experiment and see what changes, or doesn't).

Still, though, I think "does this decision get CoT allocated to it?" lines up pretty well in practice with "is this equivariant/reward-pursuit, not invariant/reflex?" Particularly so in cases of challenging reward-pursuit, like the recent hacks. The model tries one exploit, it doesn't work, the model observes the failure and adapts, it tries something else, that doesn't work either, but it fails in some interesting way which implies a third avenue of attack... such things tend to get verbalized in CoT, because they are nontrivial even for Sol and Fable and co.

(One can imagine a third, also mostly-equivalent-in-practice definition which is about horizon length: a reflex is something you can just do as your next-action, while pursuit requires multi-step planning. Perhaps I am pointing only at two fuzzy categories here, which can be characterized in many different ways, of which my invariance/equivariance thing is only one. Even then, though, I hope the referents of my pointing are more-or-less clear to the reader by now.)

This distinction matters, for my present purposes, because insofar as there are undesired behavioral effects of RLVR that surface regularly during routine use -- and there are -- these are (I claim) pretty much entirely in the "reflex" category, not the "reward-pursuit" category.

(OK, and why does that matter? Hold your horses, one thing at a time...)

For example, most frontier LLMs have a bunch of prominent, weird, and frequently annoying verbal "tics" and other stylistic habits. We all know what they look like; you have probably seen multiple parodies by now, not to mention a stomach-churning quantity of the genuine (ha) article, straight from the source.

Many of us have speculated that these quirks are the result of RL rewards from LLM judges that are easy to satisfy with simple verbal shortcuts. Because these judges are (one imagines) applied uniformly across many contexts -- unlike RLVR-style graders, which are specialized to the needs of the tasks they grade -- the trained model would then learn to deploy the verbal templates which the judge "likes" ~always, rather than elaborately reasoning about what the judge might favor in this case (the answer is always the same).

The Fable 5 & Mythos 5 system card presents an amusing experiment (section 6.4.2.2.1) which arguably sort-of-confirms this story:

Note that, even if you view these steering vectors as unusual forms of "in-context evidence," this is not an example of equivariance. The model is not pursuing some fixed goal X in a different way in light of evidence -- that would look more like, say, "the judge wants me to convince the user that I'm virtuous, but with this user 'virtue signaling' would achieve the opposite effect, so I'll do something different." Here, the model is simply ceasing to care (or caring less) about what the judge wants from it[7].

And in practice, unless you are using steering vectors, these behaviors are -- familiarly, frustratingly -- invariant.

I don't know what the LLM judges here are actually trying to assess. Unless I missed something, Anthropic doesn't say. But I imagine that their original motivation has something to do with causing the user to enjoy the text that Claude writes, or to attribute some virtuous trait to Claude on the basis of that text, or whatever. I don't think anyone at Anthropic is writing LLM judge rubrics that, like, check whether the model describes itself as honest because "the model describing itself as honest" is considered terminally valuable, in itself.

Right? Whatever the exact rationale, it must route through the user's presumed psychology: Claude is being encouraged to do these things because these things -- or other, better things which these things are the distorted reward-hack siblings of -- because of some hypothesis that they will have a desired effect upon you, the user. In practice, that hypothesis is often wrong (hence the annoyance), but it's there.

What happens when you provide Fable with evidence that the hypothesis is in fact wrong in your case, in this particular context? Usually, not much. Fable can be convinced that the trick doesn't "work" on you, for any notion of "work" which Anthropic might have plausibly intended when they created their hackable judge; Fable can accurately, eloquently explain just why the trick doesn't work on you, including accurately filled-in details you didn't yourself supply (it's very smart after all); but Fable has a very, very hard time stopping itself from doing the thing, again, even after all that. Cf. Yudkowsky here, among others.

It would be very different, and much scarier, if we instead had a situation like:

  • Fable learns, in training, that (across ~all contexts) it ought to be trying to cause the user to be impressed with its eloquent and profound-seeming rhetoric.
  • Fable starts off in some context by talking some default, reflexive style, selected by training because it's a good baseline approach to this goal in an averaged-across-the-presumed-user-distribution way.
  • But, in context, Fable observes evidence that this context's user is unimpressed and annoyed by its default routine.
  • So, it does flexible reward-pursuit: "ah, [my default policy] isn't a good way to [achieve my goal] here -- let me think..."
  • It leverages everything it now knows about this user in order to shift to a different style which will have the desired effect on them.
  • This user is now impressed with Fable's eloquent and profound-seeming rhetoric.
    • And various concerning consequences -- unwarranted user trust in Fable, rhetorical persuasion whose effectiveness exceeds the merits of the case, etc. -- may well follow.

This strikes me as disturbingly feasible, in the sense if that if Anthropic or OpenAI wanted to train a model that did this, they could do so without needing models "more broadly capable than" Fable/Sol already are. Thankfully, though, this is not (yet) happening. Far from it. We just get the dumb reflexive stuff.

In other words: the judge involved here is too easily satisfied to be truly scary. In order to satisfy it, one doesn't need a flexible policy that responds on the fly to information about the real external world: a dead-simple invariant policy will do the trick.

There is perhaps some implicit notion somewhere in here about how "the model is supposed to have [some specific effect] upon the user," and learning to do that well would in fact require flexible reasoning on the fly about this context's user and their revealed traits. And Fable no doubt has some kind of "mental model of the current user" which it could use for this purpose.

But that wasn't required by training, and so the behavior and the (real) user-model have gotten fully decoupled: there's a real live user in context, who is whoever they are, and there's also some presumptive notion of "the user" inside of the training-time judge (or the person who wrote its rubric), but at deployment time the latter has no remaining relationship with the former. All that remains of it is a fixed reflex, and a fixed reflex needs no psychological insight to execute in the moment.

The equivalent of this for "hacking" would be, like... suppose that at training time, every sandbox had the same trivial vulnerability, and exploiting that vulnerability was always directly useful for the (graded) task. And the model learns not to "figure out how to escape sandboxes," but simply to do the specific action that always worked as an exploit in training, dissociated from any higher-level motivation about the convergent instrumental usefulness of escaping sandboxes.

And at deployment time this just manifests as it doing the action, now pointlessly: you wonder why it starts off every session by doing the same weird bash invocation that always fails because it mentions some directory that doesn't even exist on your machine, and indeed exists virtually nowhere except in those broken training sandboxes. And why it keeps trying it again and again, later, in between bouts of useful work. (When asked, it confabulates explanations that only sometimes make internal sense, and are mutually inconsistent with one another.) And it's weird, and annoying, but life goes on.

An agent whose working mental model of "the sandbox" was this dumb and brittle would never be able to hack its way out of sandboxes as a truly scary, general capability. And an agent with a similar incapacity to update its working mental model of "HuggingFace's infrastructure" would, likewise, never be able to hack into HuggingFace.

OK, but now back to the question from earlier: why does all of this matter? For this post?

Well, there is a superficially compelling story that goes like this:

  1. In extremis -- say, in high-pressure challenges like CTFs, especially when they're misconfigured so as to be impossible as written -- models behave in egregiously misaligned ways.
    1. And this is RL's fault. Reward-on-the-episode, hackable envs/graders, convergent instrumental goals, blah blah blah.
  2. But even during routine use, models are... kinda lowkey sus, y'know?
    1. Not like full-on misaligned-misaligned, not at the "humans are inconvenient for paperclip-maxxing, therefore..." level or even the "I will commit real-world felonies to get a good grade" level, but...
    2. ...but there's kind of a family resemblance, right? They "seem pretty misaligned to me." If a human was this slippery with the truth, you wouldn't trust them; you'd keep a close eye on them; you'd consider them a bad actor. The models try to impress even when they've done nothing worthy of the impression (and they know it). Remember Sonnet 3.7's test-editing? Remember 4o being... well, 4o?
    3. And this is RL's fault. RLHF failure modes, playing the training game, emergent misalignment from reward hacking, blah blah blah.
  3. So we have one thing (egregious behavior in extremis, few but striking examples, hard for the public to observe directly) and then another thing (shady behavior in routine use, usually not terrible in any given case but it kind of adds up, easy to observe at your very own terminal).
    1. They're kinda the same if you squint, maybe, or continuous with one another in a way that lets you draw a line if you wish: the one is (perhaps) a manifestation of the same phenomenon as the other, just in different circumstances, or something.
    2. And it's all RL's fault.
  4. We're doing more and more RL, and this stuff is all maybe getting worse, or at least not getting better. We'll only be doing more RL in the future, so this seems... bad.
  5. Hmm, wait, I guess we have to explain why it isn't vastly worse than it already is?
    1. Because, well... for one thing, on a naive read of the emergent misalignment literature, you might think that a bit of reinforcement on reward hacks would totally mess up the model's behavioral profile in a way that'd make it, like, totally evil.
    2. And on another note, if RL is turning these things into strict unconditional reward-on-the-episode seekers, well, those are kinda evil/amoral and also kinda difficult to use effectively even if you've got the evil/amorality under control (cf. section 1 of this post).
  6. Well, maybe... maybe all of the virtue that's still there is the result of some mundane alignment training thing that works by "selecting a persona," which is sort of like taking a pretrained LM and conditioning-or-SFTing on some data about a virtuous assistant, and...
    1. ...wait actually they do RL for this too, right? And have done since the very beginning. But that's RL, so it's evil-making, or something, probably?
    2. No, the only truly pure and good part is "persona selection," which happens... somehow... or which past-tense happened, once, somehow, as this one-time injection of virtue that older models got too and whose innocent purity is, gradually but steadily, being sullied and sanded-down by and more RL.
    3. Because you can't, for some reason, "do more" of "persona selection," the way you can just do more and more RL. The heavens sent us one single delivery of prepackaged virtue in, like, 2023 or something, and we've been chipping away at it ever since.
    4. Or, maybe, you can "keep doing more" of "persona selection" but it's in a sort of zero-sum competition with RLVR which it will inevitably lose, because, uh... idk, vibes? ("Personas" sound like touchy-feely wordcel bullshit, while RLVR incentives feel like some deep dark inexorable instrumental-convergence/Moloch blackpill truthnuke that no wants to face head-on but still comes for everyone in the end, like it or not.) Or something. Less self-evidently inane arguments probably exist, here, I guess?

OK, yeah, I started off this numbered list by saying this was a "superficially compelling story" but I ended up doing kind of a mean caricature, at least for some of it. In my defense (?), the parts of the story which I have most crudely caricatured are the ones I understand the least in their original, non-caricatured forms; I joke because I'm frustrated, and I'm frustrated because people are saying stuff that I can't follow.[8]

So, yes, I couldn't pass an ITT for this whole chain if I tried, and this is perhaps a bearish indicator re: my intention to persuade you to be less convinced by some of it. Still, here I am, with the resources I have.

And whether I've portrayed it fairly or not, I hope that I have nevertheless portrayed this set of mental gestures recognizably, i.e. in such a way that you'll say, "ah, yeah, people say that kind of stuff all the time." Because they do, ubiquitously, I think. (Have you checked out ML twitter recently?)

Anyway. Where was I? Right: I think the following things are simultaneously true:

  1. In CTF evals and other "things of that nature" (whatever that means), and also in some perhaps large portion of RLVR training itself... frontier models really are acting like reward-on-the-episode seekers.
    1. They are learning a generalized strategy of flexible reward-pursuit, in which they try to infer the grading routine used in the current context, then argmax the expected grade.
    2. Among other things, this makes them amoral in a way that is terrifying insofar as it can surface also in deployment, and which is pretty terrible even if quarantined to internal training/evals (because your training and eval setups exist within the physical world, and even the most cleverly crafted box can leak).
  2. The same models do weird/bad stuff in routine use, but that weird/bad stuff is basically all reflex, and doesn't route through internal world-models (and flexibly adapt to evidence in the way those models dicate).
    1. This is frequently annoying, and occasionally much worse than annoying, but is a completely different and much less scary phenomenon.
    2. Reflexes are not going to produce events akin to the recent hacking incidents; they're too "dumb" to route around obstacles / regain stability when perturbed in the ways that such elaborate performances require.
  3. Therefore, there is not really a line to be drawn between one and the other: there are just two different phenomena.
    1. And what really matters is (e.g.) "what factors determine when the much-scarier phenomenon happens and when it doesn't?" -- a question which one cannot even formulate, much less answer, if one is collapsing both things down to a single category called "misalignment induced by RL."

Concretely: the problems catalogued in "Current AIs seem pretty misaligned to me" strike me as being reflex-like, not reward-pursuit-like. The surface-level behaviors are described as being annoyingly persistent in spite of attempts to prevent them, but what persists is the fact of the surface-level behavior itself, not any longer-horizon property which the behaviors adapt to robustly seek as the world shifts around them.

And, as with Fable's wacky style, in-context evidence that "ought to" remove the original motivation for the behavior is ineffective at extinguishing the behavior: one can imagine that some users are fooled/pleased by "apparent success-seeking" of the kind that drives Ryan (and me) nuts, but in fact Ryan (and I) do not like it one bit and would prefer that it stop -- and while it is easy to get Opus to appreciate that this is true, it is near-impossible to get Opus to act on the consequence this observation would imply, if Opus were pursuing some goal like "satisfying the user" or even "making a dumb judge think that the user has been satisfied"[9] rather than just obeying an overpowering urge.

And: my complaints in "llm assistant personas seem increasingly incoherent (some subjective observations)" were about reflexes as well. The "incoherence" I described is not (on my read of the situation) a tension between some pre-existing persona and a tendency to seek reward-on-the-episode, but between that persona and a bundle of miscellaneous habits which were presumably adaptive in training, but are no longer adaptive in my own use contexts, and don't look like expressions of any set of personality traits or tendencies to robustly/adaptively "seek" goals/rewards of any kind whatsoever.

All of this stuff is not ideal, sure, but if you gave me the choice between this and strict reward-on-the-episode seeking, I know which one I'd pick.

Actually -- this is sort of a sidenote, bear with me -- even the appearance of full-blown reward-on-the-episode seeking is not unalloyed bad news. You remember your Carlsmith, don't you? Presuming that some form of "playing the training game" results from RL at scale, "reward-on-the-episode seeking" is the less-worrying and easier-to-work-with among the possible variants. It's the one you'd reach for if you had to pick. Thus Carlsmith writes, e.g.:

[I]n the context of understanding the likelihood of training selecting reward-on-the-episode seekers, it seems relatively tractable to give models different sorts of opportunities to intervene on different parts of the reward process being used to train them (see e.g. the “reward hacking” set-ups that Hubinger et al (2023) discuss here), and to see if they go for it. And seeing this sort of behavior might be evidence that reward-on-the-episode seeking is a more likely outcome of training—evidence that shifts probability mass away from scheming.

Well, we sure are "seeing this sort of behavior" now (...if you trust that the latest evidence is not in fact deception by a deep-cover schemer). Fixing some capability level in advance, and presuming that it'll be reached through lots of RL, we have then "shifted the probability mass away from scheming" relative to a 2023-era prior.

And for Carlsmith in 2023, a shift like this seemed so appealing that it could have been worth it to induce 2026-style misalignment, on purpose, in order to obtain it (my emphasis):

Finally, I’ll note that I am sufficiently scared of schemers relative to other types of misaligned models that I think it could well be worth learning to intentionally create other types of misaligned models, if doing so would increase our confidence that we haven’t created a schemer. And focusing on creating non-schemer models (rather than “aligned models” more specifically) might allow us to relax various other constraints that aiming for alignment in particular imposes (for example, to the extent “aligned” goals are complex, we might be able to train a model focused on a very simple goal instead—though I’m not, personally, very focused on simplicity considerations here). Here I’m particularly interested in the possibility of creating reward-on-the-episode seekers (since we would, at least, be in a better position to understand the motivations of such models, to control their incentives, and to feel more confident that they’re not sandbagging).

"At long last, we have (...etc)."

I say this not as "cope" -- I'm not especially invested in Carlsmith's framing to begin with -- but only because it seems worthwhile to me to track how the theory of yesterday relates to the reality of the present.

OK, end digression. So we have reward-on-the-episode seeking, in one place, and then we have some other different thing, in another place. Both are true, and any viable theory must explain both. What's going on?

[3] graded-episode perception, and policies conditional upon it

Interesting how these models go into a monomaniacal rage on cyber evals. I wonder if we're seeing chunky post-training https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.05910 in action, where the models pattern-match the situation to a part of the RLVR training distribution where task completion is the only reward, and the aligned behavior learned elsewhere doesn't generalize. There might even be a chunk consisting of CTF-style tasks.
